entries.meaning: Rāma hesitated to speak before his mother but, understanding the moment, addressed Sītā inwardly. Princess, hear this counsel and do not take it amiss: if you wish both your own good and mine, accept my word and remain at home. My command is that you serve my mother; in every way that will benefit the household. No duty is higher than reverently honoring a mother- and father-in-law. Whenever my mother remembers me, love will overwhelm her innocent mind; then, fair one, gently console her with stories of former days. I speak naturally and swear truthfully that I entrust you to her for her welfare. By following a duty approved by teachers and scripture, one gains its fruit without pain; through obstinate insistence, kings such as Gālava and Nahuṣa endured every calamity.

Rāma continued: once I have honored my father's word, I shall return quickly, wise and lovely one; the passing days will not seem long. But if, driven by love, you insist, grief will be the outcome. The forest is harsh and fearsome, with terrible heat, cold, rain, and wind. The path is full of kuśa grass, thorns, and stones, and must be walked barefoot. Your soft, lovely lotus feet would face inaccessible roads and great mountains, caves and ravines, rivers and riverbanks so deep and difficult that one cannot see their limits. Bears, tigers, wolves, lions, and serpents roar there so fiercely that courage flees at the sound. The ground will be your bed, bark your clothing, roots and fruit your food—and even these may not always be available at a favorable time.

Man-eating night-roamers wander the woods and assume millions of deceptive forms. Water descending from the hills strikes hard, and the forest's dangers cannot be fully told. Dreadful snakes, fearsome birds, terrible wildernesses, hosts of demons, and thieves in human form make even the steadfast afraid when the deep woods come to mind; and you, doe-eyed one, are timid by nature. With your swanlike gait you are not suited to the forest, and people would blame me. Can a swan nurtured on the nectar-like water of Lake Mānasa live in a salt ocean? Can a cuckoo accustomed to sporting in a young mango grove flourish in a thorn forest? Moon-faced lady, reflect in your heart and remain at home, for the forest's pain is great. Whoever does not respectfully follow the beneficial instruction of a natural friend, teacher, or master will inevitably repent deeply when good turns to loss.

Hearing her beloved's gentle and captivating words, Sītā's beautiful eyes filled with tears. How had his cooling counsel become a fire to her, like the autumn moon at night to the cakravāka bird? Distraught Vaidehī could find no answer: her pure and loving husband wished to leave her. Forcibly restraining the water in her eyes and mustering courage, the daughter of Earth clasped her mother-in-law's feet and begged pardon for her grave impertinence. Her life's lord had indeed taught her the course of her highest welfare, but she had considered the matter and seen within her heart that no sorrow in the world equaled separation from her husband. Compassionate, handsome, joy-giving, wise lord of my life, without you—the moon of Raghu's water-lily race—even heaven is the same as hell.

Mother, father, sister, dear brother, family, friends, mother- and father-in-law, teacher, companions, a handsome and virtuous son—however far affection and kinship extend, without her beloved all these burn a woman hotter than the sun. Body, wealth, home, land, city, and kingdom form only an assembly of grief without a husband. Pleasures are like diseases, ornaments a burden, and the world like Yama's torment. Lord of my life, without you nothing anywhere in the world gives me joy. As a body without life or a river without water, so is a woman without her husband. With you, my lord, every happiness is present as I gaze upon your face, spotless as the autumn moon. Birds and beasts will be my family, the forest my city, bark pure silk, and a leaf-hut with you the very abode of heaven and root of happiness.

The generous forest gods and goddesses will care for me like parents-in-law. A lovely bed of kuśa grass and fresh leaves beside my lord will be as delightful as the couch of Love himself. Roots and fruit will be nectar for food, and the mountains will equal a hundred palaces of Ayodhyā. Moment by moment I shall behold my lord's lotus feet and rejoice as the cakravāka does by day. You have named many forest hardships—fear, grief, and countless afflictions—but all combined do not equal the slightest particle of separation from you, treasury of compassion. Knowing this in your heart, crown of the wise, take me with you and do not leave me. Why should I plead so much, my all-knowing, compassionate lord who dwells within every heart? If you keep me in Ayodhyā for the appointed term, no one can know whether my life will last. Friend of the lowly, handsome and joy-giving treasury of character and love, take me.

I shall not tire while walking the road, for at every moment I shall gaze upon your lotus feet. Serving my beloved in every way, I shall remove all fatigue caused by the journey. Sitting in a tree's shade, I shall wash your feet and happily fan you. When I see drops of sweat upon your dark body, how could there be a time for sorrow while I behold the lord of my life? I shall spread level ground with grass and leaves and, like a servant, massage your feet through the night. Gazing again and again at your tender form, even hot wind will not touch me. With you present, who could cast a threatening glance at me, any more than hare or jackal could threaten a lioness? I may be delicate, lord, yet I am fit for the forest; austerity is proper for you and enjoyment only for me. If my base life does not break apart on hearing such harsh words, it will somehow endure even the terrible pain of separation.

Having spoken, Sītā became deeply distraught and could no longer contain the thought of separation. Seeing her condition, Rāma understood that if he forcibly left her behind she would not preserve her life. The compassionate lord of the solar line told her to abandon sorrow and accompany him, and to prepare at once for the forest journey rather than grieve. With loving words he reassured his beloved, then sought his mother's feet and blessing. Kausalyā asked him to return quickly and erase the subjects' pain, never hardening his heart and forgetting his mother. Would Fate ever reverse her condition, so that her eyes might again behold the lovely pair? When would the blessed day come when, still alive, she would see her son's moonlike face, call him child and darling, summon him, hold him to her heart, and joyfully gaze upon his form?

Seeing his mother helpless with love, Rāma found no words; the moment and its affection defied description despite all his ways of consoling her. Jānakī then touched her mother-in-law's feet and called herself most unfortunate: Fate had sent her to the forest at the very time for service, leaving her wish unfulfilled. She begged her mother to put aside agitation but not affection, since hard destiny—not any fault of hers—was to blame. Hearing Sītā, Kausalyā was overwhelmed; how could her state be described? Again and again she drew Sītā to her breast, then mastered herself and gave counsel and blessings: may your married state remain unbroken as long as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā flow. Having received many such blessings and instructions, Sītā repeatedly bowed her head to those lotus feet and departed.

When Lakṣmaṇa heard the news, he ran up with a distraught and tearful face. Trembling, thrilled, and with streaming eyes, he seized Rāma's feet in the extremity of love. He could say nothing and stood staring like a wretched fish pulled from water. His heart wondered what Fate intended: had all his happiness and merit ended, and would Rāma keep him at home or take him along? Rāma saw his brother standing with joined hands, severed in heart from body, home, and every attachment. Wise in conduct, simple in affection, and an ocean of happiness, he told Lakṣmaṇa not to lose courage under love's power but to consider the outcome with a cheerful heart. Those who naturally place the instructions of mother, father, teacher, and master upon their heads attain the true gain of birth; otherwise birth in the world is wasted.
